issues.explanation: 'Dogs' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this military trauma profile: the other triggers/threat items center on interpersonal danger from men, being watched, and sudden human movements, with no supporting memory/appraisal content linking animals to the trauma. This makes the dog trigger clinically incoherent within the selected five components.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links Threat → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers, but the other selected strategies (overworking, never being alone with another person) plausibly manage interpersonal threat and hypervigilance, whereas gambling does not map clearly onto the endorsed trigger/threat pattern and reads as addressing a different problem domain.

vignette: Aisha, a 66-year-old South-Asian midwife who has spent most of her life in service, recalls the night in Vietnam when the world narrowed to a single, deafening blast. The mortar shell tore through the tin-roof of the makeshift maternity ward, sending a spray of water and bone into the air. She was delivering a baby when the walls shook and a soldier's radio crackled to life, announcing the attack. In the instant after the shock, she felt a cold, precise gaze upon her-a presence that was not only the soldiers standing in the doorway but the very weight of their uniforms. The memory of that gaze has never left her, and it is this persistent sense of being watched that marks the first trigger in her ongoing struggle. The perception of being observed floods Aisha with an overwhelming sense of danger, a threat that is always present in the back of her mind. Each time a male voice carries through the hospital corridor, she becomes suddenly alert, as if the movement of a single arm could herald a new attack. Even in the safety of her home, the mere thought of a man entering the room sends her heart racing, and the threat in sudden movements keeps her from fully relaxing. The feeling of being watched and the fear of a sudden threat intertwine, creating a heightened state of hypervigilance that permeates her daily life. This constant threat pushes Aisha toward strategies that she believes will keep her safe. She throws herself into work, attending to the demands of the hospital with an intensity that leaves little time for rest. When she cannot work, she finds herself pacing the waiting room, scanning the faces of the staff, ensuring that she is never alone with another person. The fear of any unexpected movement-whether it be a hurried step of a nurse or a sudden shift of a patient's arm-makes her over-monitor everyone around her, a hypervigilant stance that she thinks will ward off danger. In the quiet hours of the night, when the wards are empty, she can't afford to let her mind wander; the threat is a constant companion that demands her attention. Her maladaptive strategies, however, feed back into the very triggers that set the cycle in motion. By overworking, she keeps her days full of tasks that distract her from the lingering sensation of being watched; yet the long hours with male colleagues in the operating theatre mean that the presence of men in uniform continues to trigger her. When she does have to step away from her station to speak with a male surgeon, the memory of the battlefield's uniformed soldiers surfaces, and the sense of being observed spikes once more. Avoiding solitary moments with men at home has left her and her husband at a distance; the only times she can be alone are with herself, and the threat of a sudden movement of a hand or a foot in the dark hallway still echoes the mortar shock of her youth. Each avoidance reinforces the belief that she is always under surveillance, and the cycle tightens with each step she takes to keep her mind occupied. Now, after decades of juggling her responsibilities as a midwife and her marital life, Aisha feels the cumulative weight of exhaustion and isolation. She has taken on extra shifts to make up for the hours she misses at home, and she has begun to notice a decline in her own well-being. The constant pressure to stay alert has made it difficult for her to rest, and her once-vibrant relationship with her husband has been strained by her inability to be present. When she finally reaches out for help, it is not a single crisis but the realization that she can no longer sustain the loop of triggers, threat, and maladaptive strategies. Aisha fears the day she will be unable to protect herself, yet she also hopes for relief from the unrelenting shadow of her past, longing for a moment when she can trust that she is safe and simply be, without the constant watchful eyes of a battlefield that now haunt her every day.
